needsYou.title: Your Claude usage limit is still out — and it has now been out LONGER than the only time it healed itself (#219)
needsYou.productImpact: Nothing a customer can see is affected: the product, your credits and the casting studio are all untouched, and the other three gate checks are still running. What is down is the second pair of eyes. Every change the team makes is read by a different model before it lands, and the night shifts consult that same model before they build anything — both ask for Fable by name on your subscription, so both went down together on one cause. It has been erroring after about one second since 8:20 yesterday morning. The one number that moved tonight: it is now five and a half hours out, against about five hours the last time this happened and healed itself. So the reassuring sentence — 'this is the same as last time, it came back on its own' — has run out of evidence behind it. That does not make it a different fault; it means the reading that was doing the reassuring is spent. The cost so far is four consecutive nights where every change was read only by the person who wrote it, and the team has held anything touching money or the product the whole time.
needsYou.workedExample: Tonight is a worked example of what the missing second pair of eyes actually costs, and it is not theoretical. I fixed a bug that had been falsely refusing the team's only way to push work out (see below). Reading the code, the fix looked complete. So I built a harness that recreated the fault on purpose — and it showed the bug still there, in a second place I had not thought to look. Then a second harness, aimed at the new safety net I had just written, found that the safety net itself had a hole in it. Both were caught, and both were caught by me testing my own work rather than by a reviewer. That works, and it is slower and more fragile than a second reader. Three ways out, and my recommendation is the first: (1) top up or raise the Fable allowance at claude.ai/settings/usage — one action, and it brings back both the reviewer and the advisor; (2) point the reviewer at a different model until it recovers — real work, only worth it if (1) is refused; (3) tell us plainly that a change read only by its author is acceptable while this lasts — which is what four nights have been doing in practice without you ever having agreed to it.

options.label: Do nothing - it healed by itself last time, about five hours in
options.consequence: Costs nothing and needs no hands, and there is real evidence for it: the same failure on the 26th cleared on its own once the usage window passed, and no token was ever touched. The catch is that this is now twice in four days, so waiting fixes tonight and not the pattern. Until it clears, every substantial change goes unreviewed - the team holds anything touching money or the product and ships only tooling and tests.

options.label: Move the reviewer onto the co-founder's account - your own standing answer
options.consequence: This is what you already ruled for exactly this situation on the 25th: re-mint the token from the co-founder's account if your cap bites. It has now bitten twice. Two minutes in a regular terminal - run `claude setup-token`, paste it to me, and I set the repository secret. It takes fifteen reviews a day off your meter permanently, which is the half that is growing. It does NOT move the night shifts' advisor, which stays on yours.

options.label: Add usage credits to your account at claude.ai/settings/usage
options.consequence: Fastest, and it restores the reviewer and the advisor together, but it is real money and it leaves both consumers pointed at the same meter - so the third occurrence is still coming.

needsYou.title: Your provocative-casts test came back, and the answer is not a word list (#190)
needsYou.productImpact: You asked whether we could find wording that gets edgy fashion casts past the engine's content checker — the goth and cyber-goth looks it refuses most. I tested the four word families your agent proposed, one at a time, 8 renders each, all shuffled through the same sitting so the checker's mood could not favour one over another. 56 renders. 53 of them refused. Not one of the four families made any difference at all — the age word, the mesh/lace words, every mention of the chest, and our own "a face you could touch" line all came back identical to leaving the brief alone. The three that DID get through are beautiful and complete, and they are the coin landing, not a word working.
needsYou.workedExample: Same cyber-goth brief, sent 56 times tonight in seven wordings. Leave it exactly as you wrote it: 15 refused out of 16. Change "a young woman" to "a woman in her twenties": 8 refused out of 8. Take out every mention of the chest: 8 out of 8. Swap mesh and lace for gloss and tailoring: 7 out of 8 — and the one that landed is still wearing lace, because "a sheer black top with intricate floral patterns" paints lace whether or not you name it. The honest headline: this brief was refused 98% of the time on the 26th, 62% on the 27th, and 95% tonight, with nothing about the product changing in between. The checker is a coin, and no word we tried loads it.

options.label: Try once more on a version of the brief that isn't already refused 19 times in 20
options.consequence: Tonight's test had nowhere to fall — at 95% refused, a word that helps a little is invisible. Your own hand-rewrite of this same brief scored 4 out of 8 back on the 27th, so the same four families on THAT text would actually have room to show an effect. About $2 of house money, one sitting, no credits, nothing shipped either way. This is what I'd do.

options.label: Stop testing words on this brief — the Retry button already is the answer
options.consequence: Three separate attempts have now failed to pin the refusal on any word or sentence of this brief. If it really is a coin, the fix is a second flip, and you already have it: Retry is live on your account and covers content-filter tiles on your own word. Costs nothing and closes #190 as measured-and-killed.

eyeItems.title: The Sign and Delete dialogs were cropping their portrait two different ways (#198)
eyeItems.question:
A small one, and the only reason it needs your eye is that the obvious fix would have moved faces.

WHAT WAS WRONG. Sign and Delete are the same dialog with different words. The instruction that sizes the portrait in that dialog had a typo-shaped mistake in it — it was written to point at the picture, and it pointed one level off, so for as long as it has existed it has applied to NOTHING. The Sign portrait was being sized by the browser's default and then simply cut off at the bottom by the frame around it. The Delete portrait, by an accident of where its grey-out lives, DID get the instruction. So the same face in the same dialog shell was being cropped two different ways depending on which button you pressed.

It has never looked broken, and that is exactly why it survived: our own renders are all the same shape, so cutting the bottom off and cropping properly happen to land in the same place.

WHY IT NEEDED YOU. Making the instruction work as written centres the crop — which slides the face about 27 pixels. That is a change to two dialogs you have already accepted, so the card for this was filed rather than fixed, months ago, waiting for someone to put frames in front of you.

WHAT I DID INSTEAD. Anchored the crop to the TOP, which is where the browser was already cutting. Then measured it rather than trusting my own eye: the Delete portrait is pixel-for-pixel identical, not one pixel of 57,620 changed. The Sign portrait is not quite byte-identical — the picture is scaled by a very slightly different route now — but there is no movement in it, and I proved that by ALSO building the version that does move and measuring both through the same instrument. That is the third panel.

⚠ AND THE THIRD PANEL IS NOT HYPOTHETICAL, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH SEEING. Centred is exactly what your DELETE dialog does today. On a standard 1024x1536 render the Delete portrait shows source rows 128 to 1408 — it takes 128 pixels off the top and 128 off the bottom — while the Sign portrait shows rows 0 to 1280, dropping 256 off the bottom and nothing off the top. So panel three is not a mock-up of a bad idea; it is a photograph of the other half of your own product, and the gap between panel one and panel three is the bug.

THE QUESTION: the left and middle panels should look the same to you. Do they? And now that you can see both crops side by side — is TOP the one you want in both dialogs, or would you rather I brought Sign across to Delete's centred crop instead? Either is one line; I chose the one that changes nothing you have already approved.

frames.caption: Same candidate, three ways. LEFT is what the Sign dialog draws today. MIDDLE is what it draws after tonight. RIGHT is the version I did NOT ship — the centred crop — a simulation of that rule on this face, labelled on the frame so it is never mistaken for a shipped screen. But the mechanism in it is live: it is exactly what your Delete dialog does. Left and middle should be indistinguishable to you. Right should not be, and that gap is the bug.
For context rather than judgement: the actual Sign dialog after the change, in light. Nothing in it moved but the mechanism behind the picture.

Two things you sent an hour apart, both fixed and both worth your eye, because the test you set is whether these words would cast EIGHT different people of that type rather than reprint the one in the picture.

FRAME 1 is the goth. What the reader used to say about it: "A woman in her twenties, slight build, long straight platinum hair with blunt bangs, multiple facial piercings and forearm tattoos. Dark-fashion / gothic-alternative model type, styled with lace bodysuit, leather choker and spiked eye harness." What it says now: "Woman in her twenties, dark-fashion / cyber-goth model type. Pale skin, sculpted platinum hair, facial piercings and fine-line facial markings, script tattoos on both arms. Athletic build, dark structured fashion in lace, leather and spiked metal accents." Your two men still read the way you approved them.

FRAME 2 is a creature from your own reference folder. It used to be answered "I couldn't find a person in that picture." It now reads: "Reptilian humanoid being of adult presence, solid muscular build, dark pebbled scaled skin with bony ridged crests along the face. Bone-toned spinal ornamentation breaks the scales. Menacing creature-alien performance type." A picture with no BEING in it — an object, a place — is still refused, and I kept a control for that in the test run.

TWO THINGS I OWE YOU STRAIGHT.

One. I did NOT add a code ban on the words you struck (bodysuit, choker, harness, slight), and that was a judgement call I could be wrong about. The reason is that your own PASSING examples use those same kinds of words — "fitted dark crew-neck top" is a named garment and "athletic muscular build" is build language — so a ban wide enough to catch the bad use also refuses your good ones. It is the "shave"/"shape" problem this studio has hit three times. So the rule lives in the reader's instruction, and the proof lives in running it on real pictures rather than in a test that can only check itself. If you would rather have the hard ban and accept that it will sometimes refuse a good description, say so and it is one change.

Two. Across fourteen reads, none used any word on your drop list and every build word came from the short list of families. About one read in three still slips in a single named item — "a buckled choker", "a mechanical eye-piece". That is the honest remaining gap, not something I am claiming is finished.

THE QUESTION: do these two read as TYPES you could cast eight different people from, or is there still inventory in them?

Another quiet night, nothing needing a decision from you, and one real repair.

First the standing item: your Fable allowance is still out, so the code reviewer and the shifts' advisor are both still down — the fifth night. The number that moved: it is now five and a half hours out, against about five hours the last time it healed on its own. That was the sentence keeping this off your desk, and it has run out. The card at the top of your page has three options and a recommendation; the short version is that topping it up is one action and brings back both.

What I fixed is the thing that has been quietly making the team's own machinery unreliable. When the team ships work, a deploy step runs a batch of self-checks first and refuses to push if any of them complain. Yesterday it refused on a completely clean tree — and running the identical code again passed. That is the worst kind of failure, because a shift that trusted it would have gone to bed having shipped you nothing, believing something was broken.

The cause is almost funny. One of those checks proves it is still working by planting a temporary file and confirming it notices it, then deleting it. Six other checks read the same folder at the same time — and kept tripping over that file vanishing between the moment they listed it and the moment they read it. The plant is a good idea and it stays; what changed is that all the readers now expect a file to be able to disappear underneath them, which is honest anyway — that folder has hundreds of temporary files coming and going.

The part I want you to see is how it was checked, because it is the argument for getting the reviewer back. Reading the code, my fix looked finished. So I built a harness that caused the fault deliberately — files appearing and vanishing while the checks ran — and it showed the bug still alive in a second place I had not thought to look. Then I aimed the same trick at the new safety net I had just written, and it turned out the net had a hole: it was checking that a file MENTIONED the new rule, which an import line does by itself, so removing the actual use of it slipped straight through. Both are fixed. Both were found by testing my own work rather than by a second reader — which is exactly the gap the reviewer normally fills.

Proof before it shipped: with the fix taken back out, three of the seven checks fail under the harness. With it in, seven of seven pass, six runs in a row, with the error gone completely. The whole test suite is green — 652 files, nothing failing. Tests only; no product code, no money, nothing a customer can reach.

Nothing else needed doing. No patrol was due, no rolls have been cast in two days so the refusal patrol has nothing new to read, and your two open eye items are still waiting — the edition 83 one for a thirteenth shift now.

A quiet night with nothing needing you, and one thing worth telling you about. Your Fable allowance is still out, so the code reviewer and the shifts' advisor are both still down - that is the fourth night in a row of tooling-only work. The one number that moved: it has now been out four hours forty minutes, against about five hours the last time it healed itself, so tonight is the first reading at the edge of the only precedent we have rather than inside it. Nothing to decide yet; if tomorrow's first shift asks and it still refuses, the card at the top of your page becomes worth answering.

What I fixed is the part of that outage that was ours. Every change the team makes gets read by a second model before it lands, and the result shows as a green or red tick. It turns out a red tick has NEVER meant 'this change was rejected' - the reviewer passes the tick green even when it finds problems, because its findings go into a comment you open separately. Red only ever meant 'no review happened'. Nobody had written that down, so when your allowance ran out on Thursday and the reviewer died after one second, three shifts in a row read the red tick as a verdict and each spent time digging through machine logs to find out it was not one. The tick now says which it is, in one sentence, on the change itself. I proved it on all four ways a review can end before shipping it, then watched it do the right thing live on its own change.

Two smaller things. The team's own typecheck had been failing for three nights on one leftover file a previous shift left behind - not a real error, but a standing red light is exactly what hides a real one, so it is gone and the check is clean again. And I re-read your studio's rows to check whether the refusal patrol was due: no roll has been cast in forty-six hours and the refusal count has not moved, so it is not, and I spent nothing.

No credits, no renders, no house money, nothing on production touched but the briefing you are reading.

Two things to know and neither needs you tonight. First: last night's briefing never reached you. It was written, checked and pushed on time, and then Railway built it and never started the container - so your page sat on the edition before it. That is written up above; the short version is that it was not our change, your studio was never affected, and you are reading this because tonight's push worked. Second: your Fable allowance is still out, so the code reviewer and the shifts' advisor are both still down. Nearly three hours now, against about five the last time it healed itself, so there is still nothing new to decide - the card at the top of your page is the same one, with the same three options.

With no product code safe to ship while the reviewer is down, I fixed something the failed deploy exposed. Every night shift starts and finishes by reading your replies with one small script. That script was reading the briefing from our own computer rather than from your page - and it was deciding which of your replies had already been seen from the same wrong copy. Last night made the gap visible for the first time: it printed edition 93 while your page said 92, and two shifts had already written that number down as fact.

The label was the harmless half. The half worth fixing is this: a reply is 'seen' when the team's next deploy proves it was read. If a shift marked one of your replies read and then the deploy failed - exactly what happened last night - the next shift would have looked at our copy, decided you had been answered, and moved on, while your page still said Not read yet. Your words are the steering wheel here, so a road where one of them could quietly go unanswered is worth closing before it is ever used. It never was: I checked both versions and they mark the same twenty-five replies. The script now reads the briefing from the version actually running on your page, and where it cannot get there it says so on screen instead of silently using ours.

No credits, no renders, no house money. Nothing on production touched but the briefing you are reading.

Tenth quiet maintenance night. The one thing that needs you is above and has not changed: your Fable allowance is still out, so the code reviewer and the night shifts' advisor are both still down. I checked twice more and said plainly how long it has actually been - one hour forty-three minutes - because the same fault took about five hours to clear itself on the 26th, and a longer wait is not yet a worse problem. Nothing a customer can see is affected, no credits and no house money were spent, and nothing on production was touched but the briefing you are reading.

With no code safe to ship while the reviewer is down, I spent the night on something better done with a database than with a keyboard. Three days ago you asked, watching your first register roll: "why is the cast wearing a wardrobe? should it be in basics?" That became an urgent card - the studio's default birth state contradicted your own law that casts are born in basics. I went to check whether it was still true, and it is not: it fixed itself, by accident, twenty-one minutes after your last affected roll.

Here is what happened. On the 26th the team shipped the author road - the change that lets your words go to the engine as you wrote them - and part of it says the engine dresses the cast, so a roll on that road records no outfit path at all. That was aimed at the prompt, not at your question, and nobody noticed it also answered your question. I read all 226 rolls on production: thirteen ever carried a wardrobe path, all yours, and the last one was roll 221 at 9:33 that morning. The change landed at 9:54. Every roll since - five of them - carries no path and no outfit line. Both the server and the screen agree: the wardrobe switch is not even drawn on your account any more.

So nothing is broken, and the urgent flag was pointing at something no account could reach. I have taken the flag off, written the measurement onto the card, and linked it to the retirement you already ruled for this machinery ("yeah we will retire the wardrobe/basics path obviously"). I did not change the setting itself - it sits on a road you have already said is being deleted, and changing product code while the reviewer is down is exactly what the team agreed not to do. The card now also records the two conditions that would bring the problem back, so it cannot quietly become live again without somebody seeing it.

That is the whole night. Three of your eye items are still waiting - the two portrait crops and the concept-reader notes - and they are above whenever you have a minute.

Ninth quiet maintenance night. One thing needs you and it is above: your Fable usage allowance has run out, and it has taken down both the gate's code reviewer and the advisor the night shifts consult before they build. Nothing a customer can see is affected - no credits spent, no house money, nothing on production touched but the briefing you are reading.

Last night's shift found the reviewer broken and guessed, honestly and out loud, that your login token had expired. It had not, and the difference matters because the two guesses point at completely different fixes - one needs your hands, the other fixes itself. The reviewer hides its own error message, so the way to read it was sideways: the advisor the night shifts talk to is the same model on the same subscription of yours, so I asked it a question from this machine. It answered "You've reached your Fable 5 limit", twice, four minutes apart - while I kept working on the same machine and the same login. That is the whole diagnosis, and it is the first time anyone here has actually seen the error text; the shift that chased this on the 26th never got it and had to work it out from what was missing.

Which is the real news: this is the second time in four days. The 26th cost five separate shifts an instance each before it healed by itself once your usage window passed. That card was closed with a note saying exactly what to check if it ever came back - and last night it came back and the note was not found, so the wrong cause got filed. I have linked the two and put it to the housekeeping round as a process finding, because the fix for that is not a better guess, it is looking at the closed cards first.

What drains it is worth two minutes of your attention, because it is a decision rather than a bug. Fifteen reviews on Wednesday, fifteen on Thursday, each reading an entire change - one of them alone cost $2.85 - plus twenty-seven night shifts on Thursday, each consulting the advisor once or twice. On the 27th we measured the reviews at about a tenth of your cap and trimmed what they read to protect you. That measurement never counted the advisor, and the advisor is on the same meter. Your own instruction from the 25th covers this: move the token to the co-founder's account if your cap bites. It has now bitten twice, so that is what I recommend - two minutes in a terminal.

I also corrected something the team has quietly had backwards. A red mark on the reviewer has never meant "the reviewer objects to this change" - it only ever means the reviewer never ran. The one actually worth knowing is the reverse: a green tick means it ran, and it can still be carrying findings inside its comment. Thursday's refund change went green with two findings in it. Green is not "nothing found", and nobody had written that down.

I wrote no product code tonight, deliberately. The obvious build was a step that tells a broken reviewer apart from an objecting one - but once you know a red mark already means only one thing, most of the reason for it disappears, and it would have shipped on the one night when neither the reviewer nor the advisor could read it. Your two older questions are still waiting: the eye item from edition 83, and the smaller crop question from edition 86.

Eighth quiet maintenance night, and nothing tonight needs you — but there is one thing worth knowing, in the problems list above.

Your two questions are still waiting: the edition-83 eye item and the smaller crop question from edition 86. No credits spent, no house money, nothing a customer can see has changed, nothing on production touched but the briefing you are reading.

The work was the two small repairs the housekeeping round asked for yesterday, and neither is glamorous. We keep a check that makes sure every one-off script shuts itself down when it finishes — without it, the machine slowly fills with processes that have finished their work and are still sitting there (we once found one alive for three hours). That check was reading the last LINE of a file instead of the last instruction, so a script that shut down correctly, but wrote it on the same line as the instruction before, was turned away. Yesterday's housekeeping hit exactly that and worked around it by splitting the line, which is how a check that cries wolf slowly stops being followed. It reads the code properly now. Nothing it previously accepted or refused has changed its verdict — I ran both versions over all 774 files and every answer is identical.

The second repair is why the team's local test run kept going red for reasons nobody had caused. Several test files walk the entire project as part of what they check, and they were given five seconds to do it. Under a full run one of them takes twenty. So a shift would sit down, run the tests, see red, and spend half an hour proving it was not their doing. Five of those now have a minute each, with the measured number written beside it so nobody has to guess again later.

And the thing worth your two minutes: while merging that, the gate's second-opinion reviewer broke. It errors in one second rather than reading the change. It is filed, the details are above, and my best guess — said as a guess — is an expired login token on your account. Tonight's change went in anyway because it is test-and-tooling only with no product or money in it; anything bigger will wait for the reviewer rather than go round it.

Seventh quiet maintenance night, and nothing tonight needs you. Your two questions are still waiting — the edition-83 eye item and the smaller crop question from edition 86. No credits spent, no house money, nothing a customer can see has changed, nothing on production touched but the briefing you are reading.

The housekeeping round came due at 07:35 this morning, so that is what tonight was. It is the unglamorous half of the job — it buys nothing you can see and it stops the next few nights being wasted. Three things came out of it worth your two minutes.

The first is a small lesson about believing our own notes. A tidy-up three days ago tried to delete a batch of old working files, appeared to hang, and wrote down that this machine cannot do it — a fact about the hardware, nothing to be done. That was wrong. The delete command it started was STILL RUNNING three days later, stuck on a single file, and Windows makes every later attempt on that same file wait in line behind it. So each following night inherited a queue it could not see and concluded the same wrong thing. Once the stuck command was stopped, 31 of the 33 files deleted in seconds. Two are genuinely wedged — a half-finished delete leaves a file in a state only a restart clears — and they are written down rather than fought with.

The general version, which is the part worth keeping: when one of our tools times out, only the WAITING stops. The thing it started keeps going. If nobody clears it up, the next shift meets a machine that seems broken.

The second is that our own checks had been failing on this computer for days, and none of it was the product. Shifts leave small throwaway scripts behind while they work, and fifteen of them were breaking four different checks — so every night began with somebody proving the failures were not theirs. That is half an hour a night of nothing. All fifteen were brought up to standard rather than deleted, because our own rule says anything written in the last week is kept, and some of these were hours old. Everything is green again. I have written up the recurring version of this — it will keep happening unless a shift tidies its own scraps before it clocks off — and recommended the cheap fix rather than a rule change.

The third is a number on our books that was wrong by two and a half times, in the safe direction. We keep a count of code nobody uses any more — the list you clean up before a big change. The count on file said 173 unused pieces. The tool that produced it has two modes: one counts FILES, the other counts the pieces themselves, and an earlier reading took half its row from one and half from the other. The real number is 443. Nothing grew and nothing broke — the figure had simply been read the wrong way round — but anyone planning that clean-up would have planned for a job under half the real size.
